Adstock transformation as a recipe step

Source: R/steps-adstock.R
step_adstock.Rd

Applies adstock to one or more columns inside a recipes pipeline, carrying the filter's state across the train/test boundary instead of emitting missing values there. The kernel is geometric by default; the Weibull and delayed kernels can put the peak effect after the period of spend.

Usage

step_adstock(
  recipe,
  ...,
  index = NULL,
  by = NULL,
  decay = 0.5,
  max_lag = Inf,
  normalise = TRUE,
  carry_over = c("auto", "warm", "cold"),
  na_action = c("zero", "error"),
  tol = 0.25,
  period = NULL,
  kernel = c("geometric", "weibull", "delayed"),
  shape = NULL,
  scale = NULL,
  type = c("cdf", "pdf"),
  peak = 0,
  start = c("zero", "steady"),
  keep_original_cols = FALSE,
  prefix = "adstock_",
  role = "predictor",
  trained = FALSE,
  columns = NULL,
  states = NULL,
  last_index = NULL,
  history = NULL,
  seeds = NULL,
  skip = FALSE,
  id = .mm_rand_id("adstock")
)

Arguments

recipe

A recipe object.

...

One or more selector functions choosing the media columns. See "Selecting media columns" below.

index

Name of the time column, as a string. Required: adstock is a time-ordered filter, so the step needs to know the order and the spacing. The column is used for ordering and validation and is not itself transformed. It must be numeric, Date or POSIXct, with no missing values.

by

Optional character vector naming grouping columns. Adstock is applied independently within each group, which is what geo-level and panel models need. This is an explicit argument because recipes has no group awareness and a grouped data frame does not reliably survive into bake(). Grouping columns must not contain missing values.

decay

Geometric decay coefficient in [0, 1], or for kernel = "delayed" the retention rate, in (0, 1). Ignored by the Weibull kernel. Tunable.

max_lag

Kernel length; Inf (the default) uses the infinite recursive form of the geometric kernel. The Weibull and delayed kernels need a finite value. Tunable.

normalise

Should the kernel sum to 1? See adstock_geometric().

carry_over

How to treat state at the start of new data. "auto" (the default) continues the filter when the new data continues or repeats the training series, and otherwise cold-starts with a warning. "warm" errors instead of cold-starting: on a gap, on a start that does not line up with the training periods, on an unseen group and when the period is unknown. "cold" always restarts from zero, which reproduces the behaviour of a lag-based step; under start = "steady" it restarts from the steady state of the new data's first periods.

na_action

What to do about missing media values. "zero" (the default) treats missing media as no media, which is usually right for spend and is what lets a recipe run over a real, patchy panel without stopping. It is still a substantive assumption (an NA becomes a real number in the output), so "error" is available when you would rather find out. This differs from adstock_geometric(), whose default is "error"; a step has to survive resampling, and a bare function call does not. Infinite values are an error under either setting.

tol

Relative tolerance on the step between periods when deciding whether two blocks are contiguous, in (0, 0.5). The default of 0.25 is loose so that calendar months, which vary from 28 to 31 days, are not mistaken for gaps. It stays below one half so that a block one period later, two periods later and part-way through a period remain distinct.

period

The spacing between consecutive periods: a single positive number in the units of index (days for a Date, seconds for a POSIXct), or a difftime. NULL (the default) infers it within each group as the median step of that group's training index, so geographies that report on different weekdays each keep their own grid. A group with a single training time point takes the median of the other groups' periods.

kernel

The carryover kernel: "geometric" (the default), "weibull" or "delayed", applied by adstock_geometric(), adstock_weibull() or adstock_delayed(). See "Kernels" below. An argument the kernel ignores must still be a valid value of its kind, such as a decay in [0, 1] or a non-negative peak, so that a typo is caught rather than kept in the step.

shape, scale

Weibull shape and scale, both positive; scale is in periods. Required when kernel = "weibull" and ignored otherwise. Tunable.

type

The form of the Weibull kernel, "cdf" (the default) or "pdf". See adstock_weights_weibull(). Ignored by the other kernels.

peak

Lag of the peak effect when kernel = "delayed", in periods, in [0, max_lag - 1]. Ignored by the other kernels. Tunable.

start

How each series starts. "zero" (the default) assumes no media ran before its first row. "steady" starts it at the steady state of its own first periods, as adstock_steady_state() computes it, so a long carryover has no burn-in. See "Steady-state starts" below.

keep_original_cols

Should the selected columns be kept unchanged? FALSE (the default) replaces each one with its adstocked values. TRUE writes the adstocked values to a new column named with prefix and keeps the raw spend, which ROI calculations need after the model.

prefix

The start of each new column's name when keep_original_cols = TRUE: the default "adstock_" turns tv into adstock_tv. Unused otherwise.

role

The role of the new columns made with keep_original_cols = TRUE, "predictor" by default. Unused when the columns are transformed in place.

trained

Has the step been prepared?

columns, states, last_index, history, seeds

Populated by prep(); not set directly.

skip

Should the step be skipped when baking? Must remain FALSE: adstock is a predictor transform and has to run at prediction time.

id

A unique step identifier.

Value

An updated recipe with the new step added.

The problem this solves

Adstock is a filter with memory. Prepare a recipe on January to June and bake it on July to December, and the first rows of July have no history to draw on. A lag built with recipes::step_lag() leaves NA, or the filler given as its default, in the first rows of new data at every prep/bake boundary, and dropping those rows with step_naomit(skip = FALSE) removes the boundary weeks from training and evaluation (with its default, skip = TRUE, step_naomit() drops them from the training data only). step_adstock() carries the filter's state across the boundary instead, so no row is dropped or filled in.

Geometric adstock is an infinite impulse response filter whose memory is one number per series, $$a_t = x_t + \theta a_{t-1},$$ so the filter can be continued from where the training data left off. prep() stores, for each group, the training time points and the training values of each selected column. bake() runs the filter over the training rows that come before the new data and then over the new rows, so the new rows get exactly the values a filter over the whole series gives them. That holds whether the new data follows the training data, repeats its last few periods or repeats all of it.

Storage

The stored values take as much space as the selected columns of the training data, plus one time index per group: about 25 KB for the three geographies, 156 weeks and five channels of mm_weekly. They are media values only; no outcome is stored. A recipe prepared with retain = TRUE, the default of recipes::prep(), already keeps the whole training set. Selecting only the media columns keeps the stored part small.

What bake() does at the boundary

prep() records, per group, the training time points and values, and the period: the median step of that group's index unless period is given. bake() then takes, for each group, the training time points strictly before the first new row and compares the first new row with the last of them:

About one period later, or on a training time point

The new data continues or repeats the series. The filter runs over the earlier training rows and then the new rows, and the result is identical to filtering the whole series at once. A block that starts at or before the first training time point has nothing before it, so it starts as the training series did (from zero, or from its steady state under start = "steady"), which is why bake(rec, new_data = training) reproduces the prepared output. A block that repeats the last periods of training, as rsample::rolling_origin(lag = ) builds, continues from the rows before it.

More than one period later

A gap. Cold-start, and warn, naming the gap size and the group.

Less than one period later

A misaligned start, as when daily rows are baked into a weekly step or the reporting day moves. Cold-start, and warn.

An unseen group

Cold-start, and warn.

Under carry_over = "warm" each of these warnings is an error instead. A cold start begins the block from zero, or under start = "steady" from the steady state of the block's own first periods. Row count and row order are preserved in every case. The step sorts by index internally and restores the original order before returning, so nothing downstream sees a reordered table.

Kernels

The geometric kernel is the only one with a recursive form, and the only one that accepts max_lag = Inf. The Weibull and delayed kernels are finite, and either can put the peak effect one or more periods after the spend; see adstock_weibull() and adstock_delayed(). A finite kernel reaches back max_lag - 1 periods, so bake() puts at most that many training rows in front of the new data, and the boundary cases above work the same way for every kernel.

Each kernel uses its own arguments and ignores the others, and only its own can be marked with tune():

"geometric"

decay and max_lag, tuned over carryover_decay() and carryover_max_lag().

"weibull"

shape, scale and max_lag, tuned over carryover_shape(), carryover_scale() and carryover_max_lag().

"delayed"

decay, peak and max_lag. Its decay is tuned over [0.05, 0.95], since the kernel needs a positive retention rate. carryover_peak() stops at max_lag - 1 when max_lag is fixed, and a tuned max_lag starts above the largest peak the search can propose, so every candidate is a valid kernel.

step_saturation() also has a shape argument. When both steps tune one, give them distinct ids, for example shape = tune("adstock_shape").

Steady-state starts

A filter started from zero understates the first periods of a long-carryover channel. With start = "steady", prep() stores for each group and column the steady state of the training series: the state the filter would hold had the mean spend of the series' first periods been running forever, from adstock_steady_state(). The mean covers the geometric kernel's 90% effective window, capped at max_lag - 1 periods for a finite max_lag; the Weibull and delayed kernels average the first max_lag - 1 periods. It uses training media only, never the outcome.

bake() starts the filter from that state wherever the filter starts at the beginning of a training series: when it re-bakes the training data, and when a block repeats or continues the series. The new rows then get exactly the values that a filter over the whole series, started from the same state, gives them. A cold-started block (after a gap, misaligned, from an unseen group, with an unknown period, or under carry_over = "cold") is treated as a series of its own and starts at the steady state of its own first periods. That state is computed from the block's media, so a block baked in pieces starts differently from the same block baked whole.

Keeping the raw columns

With keep_original_cols = TRUE each selected column is left as it is and its adstocked values go to a new column, adstock_tv for tv with the default prefix. The new columns get the role given by role. The raw columns keep theirs, so a model fitted on the baked data uses both unless the raw ones get another role before this step, for example with update_role(tv, new_role = "spend"). A new name that is already in the data is an error.

Selecting media columns

Select the media columns only. all_predictors() also picks up controls such as price, seasonality and holiday flags, and adstocking those is rarely what a model needs. Name the columns, or keep their names in a character vector and use all_of():

channels <- c("tv", "video", "search", "social", "display")
recipe(revenue ~ ., data = train) |>
  step_adstock(all_of(channels), index = "date", by = "geo")

The step drops index and by from the selection before checking column types. To give each channel its own step in a loop, write all_of(!!ch): selectors are evaluated when the recipe is prepared, after the loop has finished, so a bare all_of(ch) selects the last channel in every step. step_adstock_channels() adds one step per channel without a loop, with a decay or a tuning parameter for each.

Tidying

tidy() returns a tibble with one row per selected column per group and the columns terms, group (NA without by), kernel, decay, max_lag, shape, scale, type, peak, start, state, state_length and id. The kernel's parameters are NA where the kernel ignores them, and before prep() when they are marked with tune(). state is the filter's state at the end of the training data. For max_lag = Inf it is the raw recursive accumulator \(a_t\), before the normalise scaling by \(1 - \theta\), and under start = "steady" it includes what remains of the starting state. For a finite max_lag it is the most recent of the max_lag - 1 training values the kernel still reaches, and state_length gives their number. Before prep() the state columns are NA.

Resampling and leakage

Stored state does not leak across a resampling boundary. Under any rsample scheme, prep() re-runs on each split's analysis set, so the state is re-learned from that split's training rows alone and describes only media that precedes the assessment set. The information that crosses the boundary is past media spend, which is genuinely known at prediction time; no outcome information crosses at all.

This step is strictly causal, unlike recipes::step_window() and recipes::step_impute_roll(), which are centred and fill the leading edge of a series using future values. Applied to a media filter, that would leak future spend into past adstock and inflate in-sample fit. The exception is start = "steady", whose starting state averages the media of a series' first periods.

See also

adstock_geometric(), adstock_weibull(), adstock_delayed(), adstock_steady_state(), step_adstock_channels(), step_saturation(), carryover_decay()

Examples

library(recipes)
#> Loading required package: dplyr
#> 
#> Attaching package: ‘dplyr’
#> The following objects are masked from ‘package:stats’:
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from ‘package:base’:
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
#> 
#> Attaching package: ‘recipes’
#> The following object is masked from ‘package:stats’:
#> 
#>     step
data(mm_weekly)

train <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$date < as.Date("2025-01-01"), ]
test <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$date >= as.Date("2025-01-01"), ]

rec <- recipe(revenue ~ ., data = train) |>
  step_adstock(tv, video, search, index = "date", by = "geo", decay = 0.7) |>
  prep()

# Row count and order are preserved; no NA at the boundary
baked <- bake(rec, new_data = test)
nrow(baked) == nrow(test)
#> [1] TRUE
sum(is.na(baked$tv))
#> [1] 0

# The filter state at the end of training, per column and geo
tidy(rec, number = 1)
#> # A tibble: 9 × 13
#>   terms  group   kernel    decay max_lag shape scale type   peak start state
#>   <chr>  <chr>   <chr>     <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr> <dbl> <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 tv     north   geometric   0.7     Inf    NA    NA NA       NA zero  1709.
#> 2 video  north   geometric   0.7     Inf    NA    NA NA       NA zero  1174.
#> 3 search north   geometric   0.7     Inf    NA    NA NA       NA zero  1504.
#> 4 tv     central geometric   0.7     Inf    NA    NA NA       NA zero  1732.
#> 5 video  central geometric   0.7     Inf    NA    NA NA       NA zero   758.
#> 6 search central geometric   0.7     Inf    NA    NA NA       NA zero  1094.
#> 7 tv     south   geometric   0.7     Inf    NA    NA NA       NA zero  5923.
#> 8 video  south   geometric   0.7     Inf    NA    NA NA       NA zero  1331.
#> 9 search south   geometric   0.7     Inf    NA    NA NA       NA zero  2186.
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: state_length <int>, id <chr>

# A delayed peak, started at steady state, with the raw spend kept
rec_delayed <- recipe(revenue ~ ., data = train) |>
  step_adstock(tv, index = "date", by = "geo", kernel = "delayed",
               decay = 0.6, peak = 1, max_lag = 6, start = "steady",
               keep_original_cols = TRUE) |>
  prep()
baked_delayed <- bake(rec_delayed, new_data = test)
head(baked_delayed[c("date", "geo", "tv", "adstock_tv")])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   date       geo      tv adstock_tv
#>   <date>     <fct> <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 2025-01-06 north  2166       556.
#> 2 2025-01-13 north  1920      1418.
#> 3 2025-01-20 north  1454      1749.
